Derived quantities from forecast draws or observed data

Source: R/derive-quantities.R
derived.Rd

All quantities are computed path by path, so their intervals reflect the joint uncertainty across ages and years. For observed data (an mt_data object) the paths are Poisson draws of the observed death counts (see mt_observed()), so the intervals are those of the observed rates.

Usage

prob_dying(
  draws,
  from,
  to,
  probs = c(0.025, 0.1, 0.5, 0.9, 0.975),
  paths = FALSE
)

asr(
  draws,
  standard = "esp2013",
  probs = c(0.025, 0.1, 0.5, 0.9, 0.975),
  paths = FALSE,
  per = 1e+05,
  exposure = NULL,
  age_groups = c("standard", "grid")
)

yll(
  draws,
  exposure = NULL,
  reference_ex = NULL,
  probs = c(0.025, 0.1, 0.5, 0.9, 0.975)
)

Arguments

draws

An mt_draws object; prob_dying() and asr() also take an mt_data object for observed rates (with Poisson intervals, see mt_observed()).

from, to

Ages (starts of grid intervals; to may be the end of the last closed interval).

probs

Quantile levels.

paths

Return the values of every path, an array [period, stratum, draw], instead of the summary (for example to compute ratios between strata path by path).

standard

The name of a standard population (see standard_population()) or a data frame with age_lo, age_hi, weight.

per

Rates per per persons (age-standardised rates).

exposure

Exposures (see mt_deaths()): for yll() the future exposures that give the deaths; for asr() the exposures that weight the rates within each standard age group (default: those of each observed year for observed data, of the last training year for forecasts).

age_groups

"standard" (default: direct standardisation on the age groups of the standard population) or "grid" (the standard weights shared among the grid cells, specific to this package). See Age-standardised rates.

reference_ex

Reference remaining life expectancy at the start of each grid interval, or NULL for the forecast's own.

Value

A data.table with stratum columns, period, mean and quantiles, or with paths = TRUE an array.

Details

  • prob_dying(): probability of dying between ages from and to (for example the SDG indicator 3.4.1 uses 30 to 70), 1 - l(to) / l(from) from the period life table of life_table() (Preston, Heuveline and Guillot 2001);

  • asr(): age-standardised death rate per per persons (default 100,000), by direct standardisation with the weights of a standard population (see Age-standardised rates);

  • yll(): years of life lost, the deaths of each age interval times the remaining life expectancy at the average age at death in the interval (see Years of life lost).

Age-standardised rates

By default (age_groups = "standard") the rates are first combined to the age groups of the standard population, as for the European Standard Population (Eurostat 2013): the rate of a standard age group is the sum of the deaths divided by the sum of the exposures of the grid cells in it, that is the mean of their rates weighted by their exposures. The ASR is the mean of these rates weighted by the standard population. The exposures are those of each observed year for observed data and, for forecasts, exposure (default: the exposures of the last training year, as in mt_deaths()). Rates of a group without exposures (all zero, or draws that hold none) are averaged with equal weights.

Grid cells wider than the standard groups (for example 0-4 for the groups 0 and 1-4 of the ESP 2013, or an open interval 90+ for the groups 90-94 and 95+) take the sum of the weights of the standard groups they cover: rates and weights are combined over the smallest age groups that are unions both of grid cells and of standard groups. Only the ages of the grid enter, and the weights are renormalised to them (columns ages, standard and per state this; an ASR for ages 50+ is per 100,000 of the standard population aged 50+); a standard group that the grid covers only in part enters with the covered share of its weight.

age_groups = "grid" instead shares the weight of each standard group evenly among the grid cells within it (the weight of the open standard group equally among the grid cells it covers) and weights the rates of the grid cells with these shares. This is specific to this package (reference unknown). Where the grid is finer than the standard groups, every cell of a group gets the same weight, although the older cells of a group have higher death rates and, at older ages, fewer persons, so the ASR is higher than with the standard's age groups: by 1.8% to 3.6% for French rates on single years of age to 100+ (HMD, 1950-2006, ESP 2013), and by more when the grid extends to higher ages, over which the weight of the open standard group 95+ is then spread evenly (up to 11% with single years to 110+). On a grid of the standard's age groups (or coarser) both give the same value.

Years of life lost

yll() multiplies the deaths of each age interval by the remaining life expectancy at the average age at death in the interval, x + a_x, interpolated linearly between the values at the start and at the end of the interval, e_x + a_x / n_x * (e_(x+n) - e_x) (as for e-dagger in lifespan_variation()); the last interval uses its e_x. With the life expectancy of the forecast's own period life table (default) these are the period expected years of life lost of Murray (1994). With reference_ex, the remaining life expectancy of a standard life table at the start of each grid interval, interpolated in the same way with the a_x of the forecast's life table, they are the standard expected years of life lost of the same paper. Neither discounting nor age weighting is applied. The deaths are rates times exposure (default: the exposures of the last training year), without Poisson noise.

References

Eurostat (2013). Revision of the European Standard Population: report of Eurostat's task force. Methodologies and Working papers. Publications Office of the European Union, Luxembourg. doi:10.2785/11470

Murray CJL (1994). Quantifying the burden of disease: the technical basis for disability-adjusted life years. Bulletin of the World Health Organization 72(3): 429-445.

Preston SH, Heuveline P, Guillot M (2001). Demography: Measuring and Modeling Population Processes. Blackwell.

Examples

x <- mt_example(deaths = "single")
fc <- mt_forecast(mt_fit(lee_carter(), x), h = 5, n_draws = 100, seed = 1)
prob_dying(fc, from = 30, to = 70)
